hints: Rewrite $y=(\cos\theta)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
walkthrough:
Differentiate with respect to $\theta$ using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = -1(\cos\theta)^{-2} \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(\cos\theta)$$

Decompose the fraction into a product of standard trigonometric functions:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \cdot \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \sec\theta\tan\theta$$

hints: Work from the left side and rationalise its denominator by multiplying top and bottom by $1+\sin\theta$.
Use $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$, then expand and rewrite the resulting terms using $\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta$.
Use $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$ to match the right side exactly.
walkthrough:
Begin with the left-hand side and multiply numerator and denominator by $(1 + \sin\theta)$:
$$\text{LHS} = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} = \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)}{(1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)}$$

Replace the denominator using the Pythagorean identity $1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta$:
$$\text{LHS} = \dfrac{1 + 2\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}$$

Split the fraction into three individual terms:
$$\text{LHS} = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} + \dfrac{2\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} + \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = \sec^2\theta + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) + \tan^2\theta$$
$$= \sec^2\theta + 2\sec\theta\tan\theta + \tan^2\theta$$

hints: Replace the integrand by the identity from part (ii).
Integrate $2\sec^2\theta+2\sec\theta\tan\theta-1$ using the derivative from part (i).
Evaluate $2\tan\theta+2\sec\theta-\theta$ at $0$ and $\pi/4$, keeping the result exact.
walkthrough:
Replace the integrand using the trigonometric identity established in part (ii):
$$\int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \int_0^{\pi/4} (2\sec^2\theta + 2\sec\theta\tan\theta - 1)\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Integrate term by term, using standard integral $\int \sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \tan\theta$ and the result from part (i) $\int \sec\theta\tan\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \sec\theta$:
$$\int (2\sec^2\theta + 2\sec\theta\tan\theta - 1)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \Big[2\tan\theta + 2\sec\theta - \theta\Big]_0^{\pi/4}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$:
$$\tan\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = 1$$
$$\sec\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\pi/4)} = \dfrac{1}{1/\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}$$
$$\text{Upper limit evaluation} = 2(1) + 2(\sqrt{2}) - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi = 2 + 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $\theta = 0$:
$$\tan(0) = 0$$
$$\sec(0) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(0)} = 1$$
$$\text{Lower limit evaluation} = 2(0) + 2(1) - 0 = 2$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value to obtain the exact value:
$$\left(2 + 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) - 2 = 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi \quad \left(\text{or } 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$$
